name: Motown & Soul
blurb: Detroit hit factories, Memphis grit and the voices that changed American music.

questions.prompt: Aretha Franklin's "Respect" added which new vocal hook that Otis Redding's version lacked?
questions.fact: Her sisters Carolyn and Erma sang backup, and the arrangement was cut at Atlantic Records in New York in February 1967.

questions.prompt: Which Motown singer's 1971 album What's Going On responded to war, poverty and unrest?
questions.fact: The title song was co-written by Renaldo "Obie" Benson of the Four Tops, who was shaken by police violence he saw at an anti-war protest in Berkeley.

questions.prompt: Diana Ross, Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard made up which Motown trio?
questions.fact: The group started out as the Primettes in Detroit's Brewster-Douglass housing projects.

questions.prompt: What name was on the sign over Motown's Detroit headquarters on West Grand Boulevard?
questions.fact: The modest house served as Motown's home until 1972, when the company moved to Los Angeles. It is now a museum.

questions.prompt: Which singer was known as the Godfather of Soul and "the hardest-working man in show business"?
questions.fact: His 1965 hit "I Got You (I Feel Good)" and his tight, rhythmic band helped lay the foundation for funk.

questions.prompt: Which 1962 instrumental did Stax's house band Booker T. and the M.G.'s record?
questions.fact: The band reportedly cut it during a break in another artist's session, and Stax later worked out of a converted movie theater on East McLemore Avenue.

questions.prompt: Which Supremes lead singer left in 1970 to start a solo career?
questions.fact: Ross said farewell at a Las Vegas show in January 1970, where Jean Terrell was introduced as her replacement.

questions.prompt: Which Motown group's "My Girl" was written by Smokey Robinson and Ronald White of the Miracles?
questions.fact: David Ruffin sang lead instead of Eddie Kendricks, who had been the group's usual lead tenor.

questions.prompt: Which singer recorded "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay" days before dying in a plane crash in December 1967?
questions.fact: Guitarist Steve Cropper finished the record after Redding's death, adding the seagull and wave sounds, and Redding was 26.

questions.prompt: Which Motown star played the clavinet riff and the drums on "Superstition"?
questions.fact: Wonder recorded most of the track himself, and he reportedly wrote it first for guitarist Jeff Beck.

questions.prompt: Which Motown prodigy, nicknamed Little Stevie, recorded the live hit "Fingertips (Pt. 2)" in 1963?
questions.fact: The take came from a Motortown Revue show, and the band shouted "What key?" as Wonder wandered back onstage.

questions.prompt: Which songwriting trio wrote "Baby Love", "You Can't Hurry Love" and "Reach Out I'll Be There"?
questions.fact: They left Motown in 1968 after a royalty dispute and founded their own labels, Invictus and Hot Wax.

questions.prompt: Which singer partnered with Marvin Gaye on "Ain't No Mountain High Enough" in 1967?
questions.fact: Terrell collapsed on stage in Gaye's arms in 1967 and died of a brain tumor in 1970 at the age of 24.

questions.prompt: Marvin Gaye's 1968 "I Heard It Through the Grapevine" was a hit a year earlier for which group?
questions.fact: Gladys Knight and the Pips released their version in 1967, and Gaye's slower, darker take followed. Barrett Strong and Norman Whitfield wrote the song.

questions.prompt: Isaac Hayes's "Theme from Shaft" won which award in 1972?
choices: The Grammy for Album of the Year
questions.fact: Hayes was the first African American to win the Oscar for Best Original Song.

questions.prompt: Curtis Mayfield wrote "People Get Ready" for which vocal group?
questions.fact: The 1965 song, a gospel-flavored plea for unity, was later covered by Aretha Franklin and Jeff Beck, and Bob Marley borrowed from it for "One Love".

questions.prompt: Which girl group, discovered at a Michigan high school talent show, recorded "Please Mr. Postman" in 1961?
questions.fact: The Beatles covered the song in 1963, and the Carpenters brought it back in 1975.

questions.prompt: Gamble and Huff's label, home of the O'Jays and Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes, was called what?
questions.fact: Founded in 1971, it built the lush "Philly Sound" with the studio band MFSB.

questions.prompt: Which band, led by Sly Stone, was one of the first major rock-soul groups with Black and white men and women?
questions.fact: They had a hit with "Everyday People" in 1968 and played a famous set at Woodstock in 1969.

questions.prompt: Which group's 1964 hit "Dancing in the Street" was co-written by Marvin Gaye?
questions.fact: David Bowie and Mick Jagger released a cover in 1985 to raise money for famine relief.

questions.prompt: Berry Gordy borrowed how much from his family to start Motown's first label in 1959?
questions.fact: He used it to found Tamla Records, and Motown was incorporated the following year.

questions.prompt: What was the nickname of Motown's cramped Studio A, where many hits were recorded?
questions.fact: The small room held the Funk Brothers, Motown's uncredited house band, who played on hit after hit.

questions.prompt: Which Stax guitarist co-wrote "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay" with Otis Redding?
questions.fact: Cropper finished the track after Redding's death and added the sound of waves and seagulls.

questions.prompt: James Brown paid for the recording of Live at the Apollo himself because his label's owner doubted it would sell. Which label?
questions.fact: Brown recorded it over a week-long Apollo run in October 1962, and Syd Nathan of King Records feared a live album would flop.

questions.prompt: The Temptations formed from the merger of two Detroit groups. Which pair?
questions.fact: Otis Williams and Melvin Franklin came from the Distants, and Eddie Kendricks and Paul Williams from the Primes.

questions.prompt: Sam Cooke wrote "A Change Is Gonna Come" after being moved by which song?
questions.fact: The single was released in December 1964, days after Cooke was shot and killed in Los Angeles.

questions.prompt: Al Green's early 1970s hits were recorded at Royal Studios in Memphis for which label?
questions.fact: Producer Willie Mitchell shaped Green's sound with a tight rhythm section and warm horns.

questions.prompt: Which Atlantic producer, who had coined the term "rhythm and blues" as a magazine writer, produced Aretha Franklin's 1967 breakthrough?
questions.fact: The first sessions for I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You were cut at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals.

questions.prompt: Stevie Wonder originally wrote "Superstition" for which guitarist?
questions.fact: Motown wanted Wonder's own version released first, and Beck recorded it in 1973 with Beck, Bogert and Appice.

questions.prompt: Motown bassist James Jamerson gave what name to his Fender Precision Bass?
questions.fact: Jamerson played on dozens of hits as a member of the Funk Brothers but was not credited on an album until What's Going On.

songs.title: I Heard It Through the Grapevine

songs.title: I Want You Back

songs.title: Signed, Sealed, Delivered I'm Yours

stories.title: Hitsville, U.S.A.
stories.dek: Berry Gordy's assembly line for hit records
stories.body:
Berry Gordy Jr. was a Detroit songwriter who had worked on the Lincoln-Mercury assembly line. He noticed that a car came off the line better and faster if each worker did one job well. In 1959 he borrowed $800 from his family and decided to apply the same idea to music. He founded Tamla Records, and a year later he incorporated Motown, whose name was short for Motor Town, the nickname of the city.

Gordy bought a two-story house at 2648 West Grand Boulevard and hung a sign across the front reading "Hitsville U.S.A." He turned the garage and a back room into a recording studio, which the musicians called the Snakepit. The band that played there, called the Funk Brothers, included bassist James Jamerson and drummer Benny Benjamin, jazz players who gave the records their swing.

The company worked like a factory. Songwriters and producers competed to write the best song, and every Friday morning a quality control team met to vote on which records would be released. Gordy often had the last word. Singers also took classes. A teacher named Maxine Powell taught manners and posture, and the choreographer Cholly Atkins worked out stage routines, so that Motown acts could appear in any club or TV studio in the country.

The first big success came in 1960, when the Miracles, led by a young songwriter and singer named Smokey Robinson, released "Shop Around", Motown's first million-selling single. In 1961 the Marvelettes, a group of high school girls from nearby Inkster, scored the company's first No. 1 pop hit with "Please Mr. Postman". The sound was soon known as the Sound of Young America: tambourines, handclaps, bright horns and a driving bass over a gospel-tinged vocal.

By the mid-1960s the stream of hits was extraordinary. The Supremes, the Four Tops, the Temptations, Martha and the Vandellas and a teenage Stevie Wonder all recorded in the little house, and the songwriting team of Holland-Dozier-Holland supplied many of the biggest numbers. The label was also notable for crossing the color line at a time when American radio and society were still largely segregated. Gordy aimed for a crossover audience, and he got one.

Motown moved to Los Angeles in 1972, but the house on West Grand Boulevard remains. Now a museum, it still includes the tiny studio, and visitors can stand where some of the century's best records were made.

stories.title: Marvin Gaye Asks What's Going On
stories.dek: The record Berry Gordy did not want to release
stories.body:
By 1970 Marvin Gaye was one of Motown's biggest stars, but he was unhappy. His singing partner Tammi Terrell had died that March, and he had withdrawn from performing. He was also thinking about the world around him. His brother Frankie had come home from Vietnam with stories of what he had seen, and American cities were churning with protests and unrest.

Around the same time, Renaldo "Obie" Benson of the Four Tops had been on tour in California. He saw police clashing with anti-war demonstrators in Berkeley, and he was disturbed. With the songwriter Al Cleveland, he began to write a song that asked what was going on. The Four Tops did not want to record it, so Benson took the song to Gaye. Gaye added a melody and new lyrics and made it his own.

In the summer of 1970 Gaye brought the Funk Brothers into Motown's Studio A in Detroit. The sessions were relaxed and loose, with the singer double-tracking his own voice, and with the musicians improvising around his ideas. The result was a seamless flow of songs about war, poverty, the environment and faith. It was also a different kind of Motown record, with strings and congas, and a mood that was gentle and reflective.

Berry Gordy was not convinced. He thought the song was too political and too different from the radio hits the company was known for. He is reported to have called it the worst thing he had heard. Gaye stood firm, and went on a strike of sorts, refusing to record anything more until the record was released. Eventually Motown put the single out in January 1971. It sold well, and the company changed its mind. It reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100.

The album, What's Going On, followed in May. It was one of the first Motown albums to give credit to the musicians, and Gaye produced it himself. James Jamerson, who played bass on much of it, was credited by name. The album sold well and became one of the best-loved records of the 1970s.

Half a century later, the questions Gaye asked still feel urgent. What began as an act of artistic defiance changed what a soul album could be, and it gave Motown artists new freedom to write and produce their own work.

stories.title: Dock of the Bay
stories.body:
Otis Redding grew up in Macon, Georgia, and began singing in church and in local talent shows. By the mid-1960s he was the leading male voice at Stax Records in Memphis, a studio in a converted movie theater on East McLemore Avenue. With the house band, Booker T. and the M.G.'s, he recorded hits such as "These Arms of Mine" and "Try a Little Tenderness". He also wrote "Respect", which Aretha Franklin turned into a No. 1 hit in 1967.

In June 1967 he played the Monterey Pop Festival in California. The audience was made up of rock fans, not soul fans, and many had never heard him. His set was a triumph, and he came away with a new audience. Not long afterward he rented a houseboat in Sausalito, across the bay from San Francisco, where he began to write a new song. Watching the ships roll in and out of the harbor, he came up with a mood of loneliness and waiting.

Redding took the idea back to Memphis and finished the song with Stax guitarist Steve Cropper. It was a quieter, more reflective piece than his usual work. They recorded the song in late November and early December 1967. As the track neared its end, Redding had not written a final verse. He whistled instead, planning to fill the space later. Cropper added the sound of waves and seagulls.

On December 10, 1967, Redding and his band, the Bar-Kays, were flying to a gig in Madison, Wisconsin. Their plane crashed into Lake Monona, and Redding was killed at the age of 26, along with four members of the Bar-Kays. The song was not finished. Cropper and others worked from the tape, and Stax released the record in January 1968.

"(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay" reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in March 1968. It was the first posthumous No. 1 single in the history of the chart. The whistling at the end, which Redding had meant as a placeholder, became one of the most recognizable parts of the recording.

The song's gentle sadness still strikes a chord with listeners. It showed that a singer known for fiery ballads could also be a quiet poet, and it left behind a hint of what he might have done next.
